clinical_reason: Older adults often receive higher-acuity review because frailty, comorbidity, and atypical symptoms can change risk.
Low oxygen saturation can point to respiratory compromise and can move a patient toward faster assessment.
Chest pain needs rapid triage because myocardial infarction and other time-sensitive diagnoses must stay on the table.
Shortness of breath can reflect asthma, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, infection, or other urgent problems.
Suicidal ideation changes safety planning and disposition even when vital signs look stable.
Intoxication can mask trauma, hypoglycaemia, overdose, or reduced consciousness.
Altered mental status is a high-risk complaint because the patient may not give a reliable history.
Respiratory rate is a simple bedside marker for respiratory distress, sepsis, pain, and compensation.
Heart rate helps flag shock, pain, fever, arrhythmia, dehydration, and anxiety, but it needs clinical context.
Very low or very high glucose can change triage priority and may explain confusion or weakness.
